title: 5. From chip to data center
heading: From chip to data center
label: Data centers
summary: Critical IT versus the facility, the power chain, cooling, and usable capacity.

spans.text: Practitioners distinguish critical IT from the broader build.
Critical IT
usually includes accelerators, CPUs, memory, server boards, racks, switches, network cards, optics, and storage. The broader project adds:

items.text: the building shell and secure halls;
uninterruptible power supplies and backup generation;
cooling towers, chillers, pumps, heat exchangers, or dry coolers;
water and wastewater infrastructure where applicable;
fire protection, physical security, and controls;
roads, warehouses, spare parts, and operations staff.

spans.text: A $40 billion server fleet and a $40 billion fully enabled campus are different objects. Analysts must state which boundary their CapEx number uses.
Electricity reaches the chips through multiple conversions:
generation -> transmission -> substation -> distribution -> switchgear -> UPS -> rack power shelf -> board regulators -> silicon.

Each stage has capacity, efficiency, failure, and lead-time constraints. The queue to connect a new load to the grid is itself a market with a price expressed in years; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's
Queued Up
series documents how long US interconnection requests wait, and FERC's
Order 2023

is the attempt to shorten it. Transformers and gas turbines can become bottlenecks because they are large engineered products with long order books. A developer may buy equipment before the final site is ready because losing the production slot could delay revenue by years.

Nearly all electrical energy consumed by chips becomes heat. High-density accelerators increasingly use direct-to-chip liquid cooling. The facility must move heat from silicon to coolant, from coolant to facility water or another loop, and then to the outside environment.

Cooling design affects PUE, water use, rack density, reliability, and where a site can operate. More efficient chips can reduce energy per unit of work while still increasing total facility power because demand grows faster - a rebound effect related to
Jevons' paradox
. The
IEA's Energy and AI report
is the best public estimate of the aggregate, and the
Open Compute Project
publishes the rack and cooling specifications that hyperscalers converge on.
Nameplate power is not productive compute. Meta's account of training Llama 3 on 16,000 GPUs, in the
Llama 3 paper
, reports hundreds of unplanned interruptions in a 54-day run, most from hardware faults; that is what "usable FLOPs" means in practice. Operators track:
For training, many devices must cooperate. A small failure rate across a huge population produces frequent faults, so checkpointing, redundancy, and rapid repair matter.
Usable FLOPs
therefore embeds operational excellence.

blocks.text: 5.5 Why power plants and buildings are built ahead

spans.text: If next year's server deliveries require 20 GW of additional powered space, the substations, buildings, cooling, turbines, and grid works must begin earlier. This creates
lead-lag CapEx
: cash is spent before revenue and sometimes before the final accelerator generation is known.
Long-lived infrastructure and short-lived IT coexist:

items.text: a power plant may operate for 30 years;
a data-center shell and electrical plant may operate for 15-30 years;
servers may be depreciated over roughly 5-6 years in current hyperscaler accounts (
economically frontier hardware may become less attractive sooner.

spans.text: This mismatch creates residual-value risk. A specialized site is only valuable if future hardware, power prices, network access, and customers keep it useful.

Data centers can create investment and tax revenue but use grid capacity, land, water, and equipment. Local objections may involve electricity prices, pollution from backup or dedicated generation, noise, water, construction, property-tax incentives, and the number of permanent jobs.

Regulation can reduce supply, raise cost, change geography, or slow projects. It can also force developers to internalize costs that would otherwise be shifted to ratepayers or communities. Most commentary treats regulation mainly as a quantity constraint; a full analysis also asks who bears infrastructure costs and risks.
